strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and practically relevant failure mode: monocular depth models can convert pictorial depth cues on planar surfaces into spurious geometry, especially after context restriction. The qualitative examples make this phenomenon easy to understand.

The proposed 3D-Mirage collection includes ROI annotations and controlled crops, offering a useful starting point for studying structural and contextual robustness beyond conventional pixel-wise depth accuracy.

The evaluation covers a broad range of monocular-depth architectures, including relative, metric, transformer, diffusion, and commercial-style foundation models, and consistently demonstrates susceptibility to the targeted inputs.

Grounded Self-Distillation is parameter-efficient (approximately 4M trainable parameters) and explicitly balances ROI correction against preservation of background predictions. The ablations support the distinct roles of the hallucination-reediting and knowledge-preservation losses.
The paper is generally well organized and provides extensive qualitative results, failure cases, training-duration analysis, and an explicit limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The most consequential issue is an unclear—and potentially invalid—train/test protocol. The method is trained using 3D-Mirage samples and evaluated on the 3D-Mirage benchmark, but the manuscript never specifies split sizes, whether the reported test images are held out, or whether all crops from each original image are grouped into one split. Leakage between crops of the same 468 source images could readily explain the very large 93.5% DCS reduction.

The dataset lacks essential documentation: image provenance and licensing, collection and filtering criteria, duplicate control, annotator count and agreement, verification of physical planarity, and category-wise statistics are not reported. Because the images appear to be collected from uncontrolled sources without physical depth measurements, the claimed geometric ground truth rests largely on manual semantic judgment.

The proposed metrics are insufficiently validated and contain serious confounds. DCS includes a sum of top-decile Laplacian magnitudes, making it dependent on ROI pixel count, image/output resolution, resizing, and sampling density; these settings are not standardized or reported across models. It also adds this sum to a mean despite their incompatible scaling. Consequently, cross-model values in Table 1 may reflect resolution rather than hallucination severity.

Zero Laplacian of predicted depth is not generally a valid characterization of a planar surface under perspective projection: metric depth on a slanted plane is reciprocal-affine in image coordinates, whereas inverse depth is affine. Applying the same construction to relative and metric model outputs after percentile normalization further weakens its geometric interpretation. No LiDAR/synthetic ground truth, human study, or correlation analysis establishes that DCS or CCS actually measures physical non-planarity or safety risk.

Metric definitions are internally inconsistent. The main text defines mean10 by discarding only the lowest 10% (thus averaging the upper 90%), while the appendix describes it as the mean of the top decile. Normalization is alternately described as per-view and per-ROI. Alignment, interpolation, mask transformation, boundary handling, and output-resolution control for full/crop comparisons are also unspecified.

The experimental evidence for mitigation is narrow and lacks competitive controls. Adaptation is demonstrated only for DAv2-L, and comparisons are limited mainly to full encoder fine-tuning and loss ablations. There is no LoRA baseline with a simple flatness loss, ordinary supervised fine-tuning baseline under matched parameter count, post-processing baseline, or evaluation of transfer to unseen illusion categories and other architectures.

Knowledge preservation is not convincingly established. NYU-v2 is assessed with a nonstandard pairwise accuracy whose sampling protocol is unspecified, rather than standard AbsRel/RMSE/delta metrics. Teacher-student background R-squared measures imitation rather than correctness, and no KITTI, driving, or ordinary planar-scene evaluation tests whether the adaptation suppresses legitimate geometry.

The safety and deployability claims are overstated. A monocular crop can be genuinely geometrically ambiguous, so a non-planar prediction is not necessarily evidence that a model ignored local geometric reality. Moreover, training relies on manually supplied illusion ROIs, but the paper provides no mechanism to detect such regions at deployment and shows failure on protrusion and photorealistic cases. Evaluated under the default Algorithms/General category, with substantial weight also placed on its benchmark contribution, these validity and protocol gaps outweigh the otherwise promising idea.

strengths: The paper studies a concrete and potentially important failure mode of monocular depth models: planar optical illusions can induce spurious depth structure, particularly after context restriction.

The proposed 3D-Mirage collection includes polygonal planar-region annotations, nested exclusions for real objects, and paired full/cropped views. These ingredients could support useful robustness research if the dataset protocol is strengthened.

The empirical survey covers a broad selection of relative, metric, transformer-based, diffusion-based, and commercial-origin depth models, providing evidence that the observed behavior is not unique to one architecture.

Parameter-efficient adaptation with explicit planarity and background-preservation objectives is practically motivated. The ablations, training-duration analysis, qualitative examples, and disclosed failure cases provide some insight into the intended trade-off.
The manuscript is generally readable and includes a meaningful limitations section.
weaknesses: The central experimental protocol is inadequately specified and may contain severe train-test leakage. Section 5.1 says that 3D-Mirage samples are used for training, while Tables 1–2 evaluate on the 3D-Mirage benchmark; no train/validation/test split, sample counts, group-wise partitioning, deduplication procedure, or held-out-category protocol is given. Although appendix captions mention a “test set,” it is never defined. Because each source image produces several correlated crops, splitting crops rather than source scenes would also leak near-duplicates. Consequently, the reported 93.5% DCS and 86.1% CCS reductions do not establish generalization to unseen illusions.

DCS can be minimized by producing an uninformative flat depth map, so it is not by itself evidence of recovering correct geometry. The appendix explicitly observes that structural collapse can yield deceptively favorable scores. There is no sensor-derived depth or plane ground truth, plane-fitting error, normal error, or independent human assessment demonstrating that low-DCS predictions are geometrically correct within the ROI.

The proposed metrics have unresolved validity and comparability problems. The cumulative top-decile term scales with ROI pixel count and output resolution, yet models use different native resolutions and the resizing protocol is unspecified. Full and cropped predictions are independently percentile-normalized, so CCS may reflect normalization, interpolation, scale, or crop-boundary effects. The description of mean10 is internally inconsistent: the main definition discards the lowest 10% (retaining 90%), whereas the appendix calls it the mean of the top decile. No sensitivity analysis, uncertainty estimates, or validation against physical geometry or human judgments is provided.

The mitigation comparison is weak. Table 1 compares a model trained specifically on 3D-Mirage against zero-shot models that were not given equivalent adaptation data. The only training competitors are a naive full-encoder fine-tune and removal ablations. There are no comparisons to simple plane regularization, standard LoRA fine-tuning, crop-consistency training, augmentation/distillation baselines, post-processing, or existing robustness methods. Thus the evidence does not isolate the value of the elaborate Grounded Self-Distillation design.

The claimed contextual-consistency mechanism is unclear. Equation 4 asks full and crop predictions to agree, but the final loss contains no explicit aligned full/crop consistency term; the paper says this is achieved only implicitly. Moreover, Fig. 4's caption says the full prediction is matched to a “more accurate” context-free crop prediction, whereas the motivating failure mode says cropped views are precisely where hallucination becomes stronger.

Knowledge preservation is evaluated too narrowly. Background R² is agreement with the teacher on the same benchmark rather than accuracy against ground truth, and the baseline's 100% is therefore tautological. NYU-v2 is reduced to a nonstandard sampled-pair ordinal score, with no standard depth metrics, outdoor benchmark such as KITTI, non-illusion false-positive evaluation, calibration analysis, or downstream driving test. A single score and apparently single run cannot support the broad claim of avoiding catastrophic forgetting.

The safety and causal claims are overstated. Cropping and resizing an image changes apparent scale, resolution, and effective camera intrinsics; it is not a faithful simulation of limited physical FOV or occlusion. The experiments do not show that autonomous-driving systems use these predictions, that phantom-road images occur at meaningful frequency, or that the errors affect downstream planning. Saying the adapted model has learned “local geometric evidence” is especially unsupported because monocular images of convincing illusions can be intrinsically ambiguous.

Dataset construction lacks information needed to judge benchmark quality and responsible release: image provenance and licensing, geographic/source diversity, annotation instructions, annotator count and agreement, verification criteria for physical planarity, duplicate detection, and category distribution are absent. Visual inspection alone cannot guarantee that photographed roads, walls, or canvases are planar.

Important implementation details are missing, including the number of planes K, ring widths, plane-fitting algorithm, gating-network inputs and architecture, lambda_F, weights for the cross-entropy/entropy/anchor regularizers, alignment and resizing procedures, input resolution, and evaluation aggregation. Code and data are only promised for future release, limiting present reproducibility.

The novelty claims are stronger than justified given acknowledged prior work on depth failures, adversarial monocular depth, transparent/mirror surfaces, and MonoTrap. The method mainly combines LoRA, teacher preservation, and a handcrafted planar loss. Evaluated as a mixed Datasets/Benchmarks and Algorithms contribution rather than purely Algorithms/General, the paper still lacks the benchmark validation and held-out evaluation essential to support either component.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting, practically relevant failure mode in monocular depth foundation models: perceptually compelling planar artwork can induce spurious 3D structure, particularly when scene context is restricted.

The benchmark, structural metrics, and mitigation method form a coherent probe-quantify-tame package. The comparison spans transformer, diffusion, generative, relative-depth, and metric-depth models, suggesting that the observed vulnerability is not architecture-specific.

Grounded Self-Distillation is parameter-efficient, modifying only about 4M parameters, and its separation between hallucination re-editing and background-knowledge preservation is intuitively well motivated.

The reported improvements are large: relative to DAv2-L, DCS decreases by 93.5% and CCS by 86.1%. The ablations support the intended roles of the HKR and NKP losses, while NYU-v2 pairwise accuracy remains close to that of the teacher.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually well supported. It includes useful qualitative examples, cross-model analyses, failure cases, training-duration results, and an explicit limitations discussion.

Although no contribution type is declared, the work is best viewed primarily as Datasets/Benchmarks, with an Algorithms/General mitigation component. Under that framing, the targeted benchmark and documentation of a neglected robustness issue could be valuable even without state-of-the-art conventional depth accuracy.
weaknesses: The most consequential problem is that the manuscript never clearly defines a train/validation/test split for 3D-Mirage. It says that 3D-Mirage samples are used for training and then reports the main DCS/CCS results on the benchmark, while later captions refer to a test set without specifying its size, construction, or separation. Thus, it is impossible to determine whether the dramatic gains are measured on unseen scenes or on training data and derived crops. Scene-level leakage would invalidate the central mitigation result.

DCS and CCS are insufficiently validated. There is no comparison against physical depth measurements, synthetic scenes with known geometry, or human judgments showing that these scores reliably rank hallucination severity. A low DCS can also reward indiscriminate smoothing or structural collapse, as the paper's own analysis acknowledges.

Metric comparability is unclear. DCS includes a sum of top-decile Laplacian responses and therefore depends on ROI pixel count and resolution. The evaluated models have different native input/output resolutions, but the paper does not specify common resizing, back-projection, interpolation, or Laplacian scaling. CCS likewise relies on vaguely described alignment and scaling between full and cropped predictions. These omissions may substantially affect the cross-model rankings.

The geometric premise needs greater care: a physically planar surface does not necessarily have constant metric depth under perspective, and zero Laplacian is not uniquely equivalent to a 3D plane. The paper should specify the depth representation for every model and justify the operator analytically or empirically. Broad, smooth but incorrect deformations may also evade a Laplacian-focused score.

The dataset documentation is incomplete for a benchmark contribution. Image sources, licenses, deduplication, geographic/content diversity, annotator count, annotation agreement, planarity-verification procedure, and train/test construction are absent. Manual identification of physical planarity from a single Internet image may itself be uncertain.

Knowledge preservation is tested mainly through a nonstandard, under-specified sampled-pair accuracy on NYU-v2 and teacher correlation on benchmark backgrounds. Standard depth metrics on multiple established datasets would provide stronger evidence that useful geometry is preserved. The undefined DA-2k measure appears only in the appendix.

The mitigation is compared primarily with the frozen teacher, full encoder fine-tuning, and internal ablations. There are no substantial alternative adaptation, consistency-training, augmentation, or regularization baselines, making it difficult to establish that the elaborate plane-mixture and gating design is necessary.

Reproducibility is limited by missing details for crop generation, data splits, sampled-pair evaluation, plane fitting, ring widths, gating architecture, several regularizer weights, checkpoint selection, and inference resolution. Results are reported without multiple seeds, uncertainty, or statistical tests.

The safety framing is stronger than the evidence: the benchmark largely contains curated street art and optical illusions, while no downstream driving stack, obstacle detector, real sensor sequence, or safety outcome is evaluated. The phenomenon is meaningful, but claims about autonomous-driving risk should be moderated or supported experimentally.
